title: Mindfulness Seminar 1
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating mindfulness in everyday life by paying attention to the present moment without judgment or distraction. This can be done through simple exercises like focusing on one raisin, observing body sensations, or listening to guided recordings, allowing us to tap into our core roots and experience a deeper sense of awareness and understanding. By practicing mindfulness, we can develop greater self-awareness, reduce mental chatter, and improve both physical and mental well-being.

So, a few things I thought of.
I think that's enough for the moment about our raisins.
The reason to do this is pretty obvious, I think, and why it's germane to this topic of mindfulness.
This is a question of whether we're actually minding, whether we're actually attending to our actual living and noticing the experiences we're having in some way.
And what a shame it would be to miss out on the flavor of life.
I was thinking of Nancy's talk a month or two ago, the flavor of life.
So there's the flavor of raisins.
And I think you brought up most of the topics that are germane to mindfulness already.
So I thought I'd give a little more background about mindfulness and why I wanted to offer a seminar on it.

And the first answer to my progression of thinking, a little bit just briefly about this: the first is just that the more I study mindfulness, the more it seems very importantly foundational for Zen practice.

And if we don't have some direct sense and experience of that aspect of practice that is mindfulness, there's a way that our practice maybe is a little bit stale or a little bit disconnected in some way.
So I've really come to feel that mindfulness is very fundamental to Zen practice.
So we're going to depart a little bit from some of the usual Zen format for these weeks and do some practices that are not commonly seen in Zendos.
But I think we can do that in the service of understanding our own tradition in a deeper and felt way.
So that's one reason: more and more sensing that mindfulness is just a foundational teaching for us as Zen students.
As Zen is not somehow sort of beyond all that baloney, you know, but is held by that.
And the second reason is, as some of you probably know, I've been studying lately in the realm of the movement to secularize Buddhism in some way.
And they're using mindfulness in a pretty skillful way as the way to present this understanding about life that comes from the Buddhist tradition and the secular world.

And so I've been studying with John Kabat-Zinn and his collaborators, studying their whole system of presenting mindfulness and their class, which they call mindfulness based stress reduction, MBSR they call it.
And I found my experiences with this mindfulness based stress reduction, MBSR, really have shifted my sense of myself and my experience in the world and Zen practice.
So that's been to me very directly important and interesting, and I haven't been studying that very long.
So I was kind of surprised.
I went from thinking, oh, well, this would be kind of cool and it'll be a nice way to present this in a different way and help people.
But as it goes, right, when you go out to do something where you think you're the know-it-all, you get out there and you actually do it and it actually changes you, right?
Like, oh, there's more to this than I thought, you know, this is actually about my own practice, it's actually about my life.
And so that's the second reason that I've been studying this MBSR.
And the third reason is that mindfulness is now sort of under the magnifying glass of science, actually.

It has been for a little while, some years in a quiet way, but now the number of studies on mindfulness and what happens with people, both their experience of their life, their physical problems, and even their actual brains, what happens with people when they practice mindfulness, is being studied much more actively in the scientific community.
It's still a tiny thing in terms of this whole world of science, but it went from being microscopic to being tiny, which is a big growth.
I'm interested to share with you a little bit of what I've learned from my time at a scientific meeting, and I've been trying to read scientific papers, which has been fun.
I haven't done that since college, so that's been fun.
I want to tell you a little bit about that because it's interesting and germane to us in some way.
And it's nice because I think we are all in some way scientific materialist people, right?
That's our culture.

So it encourages us, and I think it helps us with our practice, to know that not only did our great Buddhist ancestors say that this works, and not only do we know in our hearts and from our experience that it works, but there are also peer-reviewed scientific papers that say that it works.
So it's one more support in practice.
If you don't really feel like getting up and sitting, maybe you can think of that: if I sit today, it will change my brain.
Improve my brain.

In particular, mindfulness interventions have, I'll tell you more another week, but mindfulness has been shown very strongly in small but rigorous studies to be effective in preventing relapse of depression and helping people with social affective disorder, which is where you're so shy you can't really interact with people so much.
I don't know that much about it, but it helps.
And it's a great acronym: S.A.D.
So it's sad, right?
Yeah.
It's a sad thing to have.
Mindfulness has also been shown to help with quite a few different seemingly physical ailments.
You would think, oh, yeah, sure, meditation would help people feel better about themselves and not be depressed.
That makes sense.
But there are studies showing that meditation helps with things that seem really physical and mechanical to us.
One of John Kevitz's early breakthrough studies, he got lucky early on, and he got a really good result from an early study, which helped him keep going.
He had a colleague who was a dermatologist, and they were studying psoriasis, which is some kind of skin condition where your skin just scales up everywhere.
So it's difficult, right?
And I guess it doesn't really hurt, but it's a social thing.
Like you walk into a store and your skin's all weird.
Anyway, the treatment for it is you stand naked in this big cell.
I saw a picture of it.
You stand naked in this big huge machine, which is like this big cylinder, and these enormous noisy machines swirl around zapping you with ultraviolet radiation.
Wouldn't that be any fun?
And you have to stand in there for most of the day, I think, in shifts.
You get in, you get out, you get in, you get out, for most of the day.
And that clears it up, eventually, I guess.
So it occurred to John Kevitz, well, that seems pretty stressful.
I wonder if, in fact, mindfulness meditation reduces stress, and if a person is less stressed, if their body would respond better in some way to this treatment.
So they did a study, this was a while ago, late 70s, early 80s.
They did a study, and they found out, sure enough, and the results were pretty surprising.
Small sample again, but statistically significant: your skin clears up four times faster if you practice mindfulness meditation while you're in this light box gadget.
So that's nice to know.
That's another reason, science.
But the science is showing that, and actually there's two prongs to the science.
One prong is science showing that mindfulness meditation makes a real difference in people's physical and mental well-being and healing from all kinds of afflictions.
But then that's not completely convincing to our society, right?
You can't just say, well, this works.
I don't know how it works, right?
So our mechanistic, reductionist society, you have to be able to show why it works or how it works too, right?
So this is really lucky for mindfulness: at the same time that all the other stuff was going on, the field of neurology, the study of the mind, has completely shifted.
In the last 10 or 15 years, they have developed new tools for being able to scan and watch the brain in real time, the way it works.
They used to have to cut monkeys open all the time, right?
That's gross, but it was how they found stuff out.
So now they have new technology so they can actually watch what happens with people's brains, where the activity is, and even the density of the gray matter itself.
They can watch that with these machines.
A growing number of studies in neurology are showing that, well, we were all told, you remember being told when you grew up that once you're an adult, that's all the brain cells you're going to get.
Don't blow it, buddy.
Don't take drugs, don't drink.
Don't think bad thoughts.
Don't be mean to your mother because it's going to kill your brain cells, and you're not going to get any more.
That's what neurology thought when we were growing up, but now it's completely opposite.

Now they understand, and they all agree now, that the brain is constantly growing and changing, that new neurons are being generated all the time at pretty rapid rates, and it varies according to conditions, and that how you use your brain quite directly and actually quite quickly makes changes in function and structure of the brain.

At this meeting, I'll tell you more later, but at this meeting, one of the studies presented was, I think, the first, a groundbreaking study where they had taken a bunch of college students who had not done meditation.
They had them go through this eight-week meditation course, this mindfulness-based course, which is a structured course, and it's a fair amount of practice, but it's still just eight weeks.
There's an hour of meditation homework a day, and a long class every week and all this.
Anyway, they looked at their brains before and after with this functional MRI thing, and they could see differences in both of those areas just after eight weeks.
I forget all the details.
I've got to learn more about the, I'll get my facts straight after the details in no time.

But the left frontal lobe, which is associated with compassion and awareness and, I guess, sort of the kindness and connection with people, that was more active, and the gray matter was denser than it was before this eight-week meditation class.
And there's some change in the amygdala, too, which regulates sort of basal response to stress and stuff like that.
So, yeah, how about that, huh?
Before that, they had done studies of Tibetan monks who had, like, 10,000 hours minimum of meditation, and sure enough, they saw significant differences.
We all said, yeah, yeah, yeah, of course, those guys, sure, but not us guys.
But sure enough.
And mindfulness is the sort of aspect of meditation that's being studied in all these cases.
So I thought that would be another good reason to study mindfulness in some more or less structured and systematic way with you together for six weeks.

So what do we mean by mindfulness?
It says right on here.
Well, mindfulness is an English word, of course, so we need to unpack how it's being used here and where it came from and what it actually means to practice mindfulness.
Mindfulness is from the word mindful, which in the dictionary means attentive, aware, or careful.
And in English, it seems to always imply a subject.
You're mindful of something, as in mindful of holding on to something you're trying to remember, like remembering something has that quality.
I guess it was first seen in the English language in about the 14th century.
And so the sense is that the mind is full of something, mindful, right?
The mind is full of something, some cognitive content.
And we use it that way, right?
"Oh, I'm not being very mindful.
I forgot where I put my keys," or something.
So that English word, with that sense of remembering and holding something in mind, was used as a translation for a Pali or a Sanskrit term, for a Buddhist term.
And that term in Pali is sati.
That's what you hear more often.
We have two canonical languages in Buddhism, right?
There's Pali and Sanskrit, and then all the secondary languages, Tibetan, Japanese, Chinese, and so on.
So we tend to use a mix of Pali and Sanskrit, because it's a little confusing.
Like dharma is Sanskrit.
Dhamma is Pali.
There's also a Sanskrit version of this word, which is smrti.
Sounds like smurfs.
So I guess they use sati instead.
This sati, which got translated as mindfulness in Buddhism, has much more of a sense of process and less of a sense of content or object.
What it seems to mean in Buddhism is holding the attention in a certain way.
Usually when holding the attention, there is an object, but the object is not held inside the mind as if it could be contained by the mind, or as if the mind was full of it.
It's more like the attention is held gently against the object.
And so we can practice mindfulness of breathing, right?
So there's mindfulness, a process, and breathing, an object, which is also a process.
And we can hold the attention against the breathing.
But I think where it starts to differ from the conventional English usage is that we recognize the subject-object divide there as just a convention.

As we practice holding the attention against this object of breathing or whatever it is, and we'll talk about several different objects that we could practice mindfulness [unclear: "cooperation"] with, as you're holding the awareness against that object, you start to feel and experience, experientially, that those boundaries are much more porous than you thought.
You know what I mean?

As you practice mindfulness of breathing, I think all of us that have some shade of experience around this, sometimes it seems like, "Oh, this is me watching my breathing, some little thing down there going up and down, in and out, some machine down there."
But sometimes as we engage more fully and more gently with mindfulness of breathing, there's just a sense of just breathing.
And there's no you really watching that breathing.
The subject and the object kind of merge together in some way.
Or maybe there's some sense of breathing is breathing you.
Or it alternates and shifts around in some way.
And so mindfulness practice has this sense of gently and persistently holding awareness in a certain way, deliberately, against an object, and just allowing that experience to unfold the way it will.
And, most importantly, not to add anything else to that experience.
Not to add anything else to that experience.
So not adding judgments.
Not adding narrative.
And if we notice, and we have some examples of that in a raisin exercise, right?
We started with awareness of the raisin, and then we're thinking about something else, and then we realize we're not actually here.
It's not to say that mindfulness never ceases to function, exactly.
It doesn't seem to really be correct to say, "I was mindful of the breathing, and then I screwed up."

It's more that I was holding the attention against the breathing, and then the attention moved to the thinking, and then the attention was lost to my cognition because I got really caught in the story.
And then I was able to bring the attention back to the breathing.
So that whole arc of experience is the practice of mindfulness of breathing.
It's the holding of the attention in a certain non-judgmental, deliberate way.
John Kabat-Zinn has a definition, which I'll bring in a handout, too, which is something like, mindfulness is employing the attention in a deliberate way without judgment.
So there's deliberateness, non-judgment, and, well, those two, mostly.
And so how does this appear in Buddhism, we might ask.
Where did this come from?
These things don't just come out of the air.
I'm going to say a little more, and then I want to do another mindfulness experiment before we run out of time.
So there are two, it's okay, two places.
Mindfulness shows up on two really core early Buddhist lists, and then it shows up most clearly explicated in two early Buddhist sutras.

The two early Buddhist lists where mindfulness, this word sati in Pali, shows up: one is the Eightfold Noble Path, which is itself the fourth of the Four Ennobling Truths, which are supposed to be what the Buddha first ever thought of.
So the story, briefly, goes like this.
The Buddha had this incredible enlightenment experience, right?
He could really see things the way they are.
He was really freed from the patterns of reactivity and suffering.
It was just crystal clear.
And then after some internal stuff, he decided, okay, well, I'll try to go teach this.
I'll try to see if I can explain this to somebody.
The first person he ran into was a merchant walking from point A to point B, who saw the Buddha and was impressed in some way with his energy and said, "Wow, who are you?
What is your practice?
Who do you study with?"
And the Buddha said something like, "I have no teacher.
I am myself the world-honored one.
I have done all that can be done and am freed from the bonds of suffering."
And the guy said, "Oh, good for you."
That's what it says in the early...
He said something like, "Oh, good for you," and kept walking.
So the Buddha had to figure out some way to formulate this and say it in a way that people would actually listen and then practice, so that they themselves could have some experience of it.
You can't just say something, right?
And we've all experienced that, right?
After your wonderful realizations of the Long Zen retreat, you go home and you're all excited to tell your spouse or your partner or something, and they're like, "Would you take out the garbage?"
So it's the same thing.
His second run at this was a teaching on a set of four points, the Four Noble Truths, they call them later, or the Four Ennobling Truths.
Essentially they lay out a system of how there is suffering and dissatisfaction in life, fully acknowledging that as the first point, the second point being what the mechanism is that creates that.
So first is recognizing the reality of this suffering and dissatisfaction with life, which operates at many subtle levels, even if things are basically fine, right?
Recognition of that.
The second is understanding of the mechanism and why that happens.
The third is that you really can do something about it.
You really can do something about it, which is important, right?
And the fourth is: here's what you do.
That fourth one, here's what you do, was a list of eight.
He had eight points in what you should do.
So mindfulness is one of those eight points.
That's pretty good billing.
And then the second place it shows up is a list, a little bit later, I guess.
There's a list of seven, which they call the seven factors of enlightenment, seven attitudes and practices that you should take up to continue with your practice in a productive way.
I'll tell you what else the seven are another time.
So anyway, mindfulness shows up really early in Buddhism, at the beginning.
And then there are two sutras in which he explicates how you practice that, how you actually do it.
So maybe his whole forty years of teaching was sort of recovering from that one moment with that guy, you know?
"Damn!
I've got to figure out how to do this here."
It's a great part of the Buddhist story, I think.
The first one, the most famous and the longest, is called the Satipatthana Sutta.
So there's sati, you can hear it right at the beginning of that, Satipatthana Sutta, which in English is called the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.
And the second is the Anapanasati.
So there's sati again.
Anapanasati Sutta, the sutra on the mindfulness of breathing.
It goes into more detail about mindfulness of breathing.
I'm going to talk a little bit about the sutras, not too much, over the course of our seminar.
I'm mostly interested in actual experiential practice, so I'm going to try to restrain myself from the exciting and interesting textual things.
But if you want to get into it, I recommend all these books.
I'll tell you the books I'm working from, and this will be in the notes on the website, too.
The first is a book by Thich Nhat Hanh, titled Transformation and Healing, subtitled Sutra on the Four Establishments of Mindfulness.
You can look at these after, too.
As his books are, it's a very sweet and somewhat interpretive translation, with some really lovely suggestions on how to practice.
The second book I'm going to be looking at is called The Four Foundations of Mindfulness.
It's by an American monk named U Silananda, and it's a much more literal translation, so I always like to have both.
The third book I like, which is newer to me, I'm just studying it now, is a book called Breath by Breath: The Liberating Practice of Insight Meditation by Larry Rosenberg.
He's actually teaching on the second of those suttas, the Anapanasati Sutta, and it seems like a very wonderful book.
He's done Zen practice and Vipassana practice, too, so he's a good bridge builder for us.
So I'm going to end our evening.
We've got about 25 minutes left.
I want to end our evening with a mindfulness practice and suggest that you also try this practice at home for the rest of the week until we meet again.
But first I want to make two overall points about investigating and studying mindfulness.
The first, which Larry Rosenberg pointed out, is that mindfulness is an experience.
We need words and concepts and designations.
That's how we think and how we operate.
But mindfulness is not the word mindfulness.
It's not the idea of mindfulness.
It's not the book about mindfulness.
It's an actual lived experience felt in the body.
So that's the first thing.

That's one thing I think we can just remind ourselves of: the only way that mindfulness practice could actually change or shift our understanding or heal us in some ways is if we actually experience it.
Probably changing our thinking a little bit is helpful.
But changing our thinking is most useful as a support for actually changing our actions, actually choosing to take up practice.
So that's the first thing: mindfulness is an experience.
And the second thing is that mindfulness, like Zen too, is really simple.
It's really simple.
And so part of our study of mindfulness I think is studying the constellation of resistances that arise out of simplicity.
They were basically deeply conditioned to think that something simple is essentially probably dumb, probably not effective, because complicated things are effective, and so on and so forth.

So just notice if we have resistance to the simplicity of it, and watch the mind pulling away from very simple mindfulness practice, like watching the breathing, watching the body, with some story and reaction to the simplicity of it, or just some sort of lack of ability to actually have faith in something that simple.
How can something that simple?
I went to school for X many years.
How can something that simple make a difference?
That's something we work with in Zen.
Neither of these things are new to us, I think.
Practice is experiential in that its core roots are very simple.
